x.ASV: Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth; their idols are upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: the things that ye carried about are made a load, a burden to the weary beast.
x.Darby: Bel is bowed down, Nebo bendeth; their idols are upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: the things ye carried are laid on, a burden to the weary [beast].
x.KJV: Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth, their idols were upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: your carriages were heavy loaden; they are a burden to the weary beast.
x.YLT: Bowed down hath Bel, stooping is Nebo, Their idols have been for the beast and for cattle, Your burdens are loaded, a burden to the weary.

nt: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Bel and Nebo both bow low]
The words **Bel** and **Nebo** are the names of Babylonian gods.

The implication is that the images of these gods are being loaded onto the pack animals to be carried away into captivity. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [their images are loaded onto animals and beasts]
The pronoun **your** refers to the people of Babylon, whose idols these are. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Babylon’s carried things are loaded]

The expression **loaded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they have loaded your carried things]

Isaiah is using the adjective **weary** as a noun to mean a certain kind of animal. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to those who are weary]

x.ASV: They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden, but themselves are gone into captivity.
x.Darby: They bend, they are bowed down together; they could not deliver the burden, and themselves are gone into captivity.
x.KJV: They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden, but themselves are gone into captivity.
x.YLT: They have stooped, they have bowed together, They have not been able to deliver the burden, And themselves into captivity have gone.

nt: The terms **stooped** and **bowed down** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They completely bowed down together]
The pronoun **They** refers to the idols of Bel and Nebo. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The idols of Bel and Nebo stooped]

The implication is that these gods could not even save their own images, which are the burden being carried away. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they were not able to rescue even their own images]

Isaiah is speaking as if these idols each had a **soul**, and he is using that part of them to mean all of them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they have gone]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [away as captives]

x.ASV: Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, that have been borne by me from their birth, that have been carried from the womb;
x.Darby: Hearken unto me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, ye who have been borne from the belly, who have been carried from the womb:
x.KJV: Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb:
x.YLT: Hearken unto Me, O house of Jacob, And all the remnant of Israel, Who are borne from the belly, Who are carried from the womb,

nt: Here, **house of Jacob** represents “the people who are descended from Jacob.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people descended from Jacob]

Here, **the house of Israel** represents “the people who are descended from Israel.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

The terms **house of Jacob** and **house of Israel** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [those remaining of the descendants of Jacob, who is Israel]

The terms **the ones loaded from the belly** and **the ones carried from the womb** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [you who I have carried since your birth]

x.ASV: and even to old age I am he, and even to hoar hairs will I carry you; I have made, and I will bear; yea, I will carry, and will deliver.
x.Darby: Even to old age, I [am] HE, and unto hoary hairs I will carry [you]: It is I that have made, and I will bear, and I will carry, and will deliver.
x.KJV: And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you.
x.YLT: Even to old age I am He, and to grey hairs I carry, I made, and I bear, yea, I carry and deliver.

nt: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will bear** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his commitment to uphold Israel. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself will bear you]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [And because I, Yahweh, made you, I myself will bear you]

For poetic purposes, Isaiah is using two different words that have basically the same meaning. The ULT translates the one here as **carry** and the one in verses 1 and 3 as “carried” because English does not have two different words that it can use in this context. But if your language does, it would be appropriate to use them here.

x.ASV: To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like?
x.Darby: To whom will ye liken me and make me equal, or compare me, that we may be like?
x.KJV: To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like?
x.YLT: To whom do ye liken Me, and make equal? And compare Me, that we may be like?

nt: Yahweh is using the question form to assert that there is no one who can be compared to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one to whom you can liken me, that you should equate me, and no one to whom you can compare me, that we should resemble.]

x.ASV: Such as lavish gold out of the bag, and weigh silver in the balance, they hire a goldsmith, and he maketh it a god; they fall down, yea, they worship.
x.Darby: — They lavish gold out of the bag, and weigh silver in the balance; they hire a goldsmith, and he maketh it agod: they fall down, yea, they worship.
x.KJV: They lavish gold out of the bag, and weigh silver in the balance, and hire a goldsmith; and he maketh it a god: they fall down, yea, they worship.
x.YLT: --They are pouring out gold from a bag, And silver on the beam they weigh, They hire a refiner, and he maketh it a god, They fall down, yea, they bow themselves.

nt: By **The ones dumping gold**, Isaiah means that people who want an idol pour out gold freely and lavishly to pay for their idol to be made. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [To obtain an idol to worship, the people lavishly pouring out gold]
The phrase **The ones** refers to people in general who make idols to worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people dumping gold]

The implication is that the object they make is merely a manufactured image, even though they call it a god and worship it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they make it into an idol that they call a god]

The pronoun **it** refers to the **gold** and **silver** that they provided to the metalworker. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the metalworker makes the metals]

x.ASV: They bear it upon the shoulder, they carry it, and set it in its place, and it standeth, from its place shall it not remove: yea, one may cry unto it, yet can it not answer, nor save him out of his trouble.
x.Darby: They bear him on the shoulder, they carry him, and set him in his place; there he standeth, he doth not remove from his place: yea, one crieth unto him, and he answereth not; he saveth him not out of his trouble.
x.KJV: They bear him upon the shoulder, they carry him, and set him in his place, and he standeth; from his place shall he not remove: yea, one shall cry unto him, yet can he not answer, nor save him out of his trouble.
x.YLT: They lift him up on the shoulder, They carry him, and cause him to rest in his place, And he standeth, from his place he moveth not, Yea, one crieth unto him, and he answereth not, From his adversity he saveth him not.

nt: The pronoun **They** refers to the people who make and worship the idol. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people who make the idol lift it]

Isaiah is speaking of the idol as if it were a living thing that could **stand** and **depart**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it remains there; it does not move from its place]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [And one cries out to it]

Isaiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between all that people do to set up and call upon the idol and the idol’s complete inability to answer or save them. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [yet it does not answer]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the difficult situation he is in]

x.ASV: Remember this, and show yourselves men; bring it again to mind, O ye transgressors.
x.Darby: Remember this, and shew yourselves men; call it to mind, ye transgressors.
x.KJV: Remember this, and shew yourselves men: bring it again to mind, O ye transgressors.
x.YLT: Remember this, and shew yourselves men, Turn it back, O transgressors, to the heart.

nt: Yahweh is using the phrase **return {it}, rebelling ones, to the heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “think carefully about this.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [think carefully about this, you rebels]

The pronoun **it** refers to what Yahweh is telling the people to remember, namely that he alone is God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [return the truth that I alone am God]

x.ASV: Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me;
x.Darby: Remember the former things of old; for I [am]God, and there is none else; [I am]God, and there is none like me;
x.KJV: Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me,
x.YLT: Remember former things of old, For I am Mighty, and there is none else, God--and there is none like Me.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **eternity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from before time began]
כִּ֣י אָנֹכִ֥י אֵל֙ וְ⁠אֵ֣ין ע֔וֹד אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְ⁠אֶ֥פֶס כָּמֽוֹ⁠נִי

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [for I am God and there is no other; indeed, none is like me]

In the phrase **God, and none is like me**, God is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I am God, and none is like me]

x.ASV: declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things that are not yet done; saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure;
x.Darby: declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure;
x.KJV: Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
x.YLT: Declaring from the beginning the latter end, And from of old that which hath not been done, Saying, `My counsel doth stand, And all My delight I do.'

nt: Yahweh is referring to all of history by naming its two major components, **the end** and **the beginning**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [declaring what will happen from beginning to end]

The expression **have not been done** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [what has not yet happened]

Yahweh is speaking of his **counsel** as if it were a living thing that could **stand**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My counsel will be established]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [What I have decided]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I want]

x.ASV: calling a ravenous bird from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country; yea, I have spoken, I will also bring it to pass; I have purposed, I will also do it.
x.Darby: calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. Yea, I have spoken, I will also bring it to pass; I have purposed it, I will also do it.
x.KJV: Calling a ravenous bird from the east, the man that executeth my counsel from a far country: yea, I have spoken it, I will also bring it to pass; I have purposed it, I will also do it.
x.YLT: Calling from the east a ravenous bird, From a far land the man of My counsel, Yea, I have spoken, yea, I bring it in, I have formed it, yea, I do it.

nt: Yahweh is using **the rising {of the sun}** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the east.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the eastern direction]

Yahweh is speaking of the conqueror he will summon as if he were **a bird of prey**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [one who will quickly defeat his enemies]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **land** that is characterized by being far away. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from a faraway land]

The implication is that this is the man whom Yahweh has chosen to carry out his plan. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the man whom I have chosen to carry out my plan]
See how you translated the similar expression in [46:10](../46/10.md).

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Surely, I have spoken]

Yahweh is repeating the word **Indeed** in order to strongly intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Surely, I have spoken; certainly, I will make it come about. I have formed it; You can be sure that I will do it]
